ect.label: ECT Suite

inductionAgents.notes: Gold standard — minimal seizure threshold elevation
Higher seizure threshold — may need higher stimulus charge
Best for cardiac patients; may prolong seizure

muscleRelaxants.notes: Standard — modifies seizure to prevent injury
If sux contraindicated; reverse with sugammadex 16 mg/kg

drugCautions: ⚠ AVOID lidocaine pre-treatment — raises seizure threshold significantly
Glycopyrrolate 0.2 mg or atropine 0.4 mg pre-procedure to prevent vagal bradycardia
Esmolol 0.5-1 mg/kg IV or labetalol 5-10 mg IV available for post-ictal hypertension/tachycardia
NSAID (ketorolac 30 mg) post-procedure for myalgia/headache — if no contraindication
Caffeine 500-1000 mg IV may augment seizure if inadequate (rarely needed)
procedureConcerns: Brief generalised seizure (30-90 sec target) — check EEG quality
Hyperdynamic response post-ictal — particularly risky in CAD/aortic aneurysm
Series of treatments (typically 6-12) — track cumulative effects + memory
Bite injury risk — bite block + jaw support during stimulation
Pacemaker/ICD: notify cardiology — disable ICD if defib function active
equipmentChecklist: Emergency drug cart (atropine, adrenaline, ephedrine, glycopyrrolate, sux)

recovery.warnings: Watch for post-ictal confusion, headache, transient memory impairment, myalgia

redFlags: Raised ICP / intracranial mass / recent neurosurgery
specialPopulations: Pregnancy — ECT considered safe in 2nd/3rd trimester (left lateral tilt, avoid hyperventilation)
Elderly — reduced doses; watch for prolonged confusion
ect.references: Royal College of Psychiatrists ECT Handbook 2019; ANZCA PS09 2024; Hermann RC. Am J Psychiatry 2008

cardiac_cath.label: Cardiac Cath Lab
cardiac_cath.description: Coronary intervention, structural heart procedures, electrophysiology

procedureSpecific.summary: Wolff-Parkinson-White accessory-pathway ablation. Distinct from AF/AVNRT ablation: avoid AV-nodal blockers (would accelerate conduction through accessory pathway in pre-excited AF → VF risk), keep anaesthetic light enough to permit inducible tachycardia, expect isoproterenol-induced tachycardia.
procedureSpecific.preferredTechnique: Conscious sedation OR light general anaesthesia. TIVA preferred over volatile (cleaner cardiac electrophysiology). Avoid muscle relaxants beyond intubation (phrenic mapping for left-sided pathways).
drugsToAvoid: Verapamil, diltiazem (IV) — CONTRAINDICATED in pre-excited AF (may accelerate accessory-pathway conduction → VF)
Digoxin — same mechanism; absolutely avoided in WPW with AF history
Adenosine — caution: may convert to pre-excited AF; reserve for narrow-QRS SVT only, with EP team and defibrillator ready
IV β-blocker bolus — relative avoidance during ablation; theoretical risk of promoting accessory-pathway conduction in pre-excited AF
Ketamine — relative avoidance: sympathetic surge may abolish inducibility and is poorly tolerated in haemodynamically marginal patients
Deep volatile anaesthesia (>1 MAC sevoflurane) — suppresses accessory-pathway conduction, reduces inducibility (Sharpe 1995)
Routine intra-procedure muscle relaxant re-dosing — interferes with phrenic-nerve mapping for left-sided / right free-wall pathways
Amiodarone IV in pre-excited AF — contested; ESC 2019 cautions that AV-nodal slowing may worsen ventricular rate; defer to EP team
drugsPreferred: Propofol TIVA at low-moderate rate (50–100 mcg/kg/min) — minimal EP effect at clinical doses, fully titratable
Remifentanil infusion 0.05–0.15 mcg/kg/min — opioid-sparing, no accumulation, no AV-nodal effect
Dexmedetomidine 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/h infusion — particularly useful (does not abolish inducibility, no respiratory depression)
Fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg titrated — for analgesia at sheath insertion
Midazolam 1–2 mg IV titrated — anxiolysis only, avoid heavy benzodiazepine load
monitoringEmphasis: Defibrillator pads applied BEFORE sedation — pre-excited AF risk
Invasive arterial line if patient haemodynamically borderline, otherwise NIBP every 3 min
EtCO₂ via nasal cannula if conscious sedation; full capnography if airway secured
Femoral access sites — observe for haematoma
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Pre-excited AF during procedure: do NOT give AV-nodal blockers. Synchronised DC cardioversion 100–200 J biphasic if haemodynamically unstable. Procainamide 10 mg/kg IV over 20 min if stable (slows accessory pathway).
⚠ Isoproterenol 1–4 mcg/min IV provocation expected — anticipate tachycardia (HR 120–160), transient hypotension; avoid blocking effect with β-blockers
Phrenic-nerve injury risk for left-sided pathways and right free-wall pathways near phrenic — ensure no neuromuscular block during mapping
Cardiac tamponade risk from transseptal puncture — pericardiocentesis kit ready
Tachycardia-induced hypotension during induced AVRT — transient, usually self-terminates with overdrive pacing or DC cardioversion
Long procedure (90–180 min) — DVT prophylaxis with intermittent pneumatic compression, padding, careful positioning
procedureSpecific.crisisPlan: Pre-excited AF with haemodynamic compromise → immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (100→200 J biphasic). Stable pre-excited AF → procainamide 10 mg/kg IV over 20 min OR ibutilide 1 mg IV (not amiodarone — slow AV nodal blockade may worsen). Cardiac tamponade → emergency pericardiocentesis ± transfer to OR for surgical drainage.
patientSelection: High-risk WPW (short refractory period < 250 ms, multiple pathways, history of pre-excited AF or syncope) — anticipate haemodynamic instability
Paediatric WPW — almost always GA with TIVA; avoid sympathomimetics, full airway management
Pregnant patient with WPW — defer ablation if possible; if essential, consider procedure under regional cover with shielded fluoroscopy minimal use
Concomitant structural heart disease (Ebstein anomaly common with right-sided pathways) — full GA, invasive monitoring, cardiothoracic backup
procedureSpecific.references: Brugada J et al. ESC/EHRA SVT Guidelines 2019, Eur Heart J 2020;41:655 (PMID 31504425). Cohen MI et al. PACES/HRS Expert Consensus on Asymptomatic WPW. Heart Rhythm 2012;9:1006 (PMID 22579340). SCAI 2024 Cath Lab Sedation Guidelines.

additional: Arterial line (TAVI, MitraClip, Impella, lead extraction)
Central venous access (TAVI, severe LV dysfunction)
TEE probe (TAVI, MitraClip, LAA closure, ASD/VSD)

inductionAgents.notes: Deep sedation; titrate carefully in low EF
Preferred induction in severe AS / cardiogenic shock

inductionAgents.dose: Load 1 mcg/kg over 10 min, infusion 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h
inductionAgents.notes: Useful for EP procedures (no respiratory depression)

drugCautions: Heparin 70-100 IU/kg loading IV — target ACT 250-300 sec (PCI), 250-350 (TAVI/MitraClip)
Bivalirudin alternative if HIT — bolus 0.75 mg/kg + infusion 1.75 mg/kg/h
Protamine 1 mg per 100 IU residual heparin (slow IV — cap 50 mg single dose)
Contrast nephropathy prophylaxis: hold ACEi/ARB 24h pre, hold metformin 48h post, IV hydration 1 mL/kg/h
Antiplatelet continuation (aspirin/clopidogrel) — do NOT stop before PCI
⚠ Contrast allergy: pre-medicate prednisolone 30 mg PO 13h, 7h, 1h pre + diphenhydramine 50 mg
Rapid pacing during TAVI deployment → expect transient profound hypotension; ensure phenylephrine/noradrenaline ready
EP ablation: avoid muscle relaxant beyond intubation (interferes with phrenic nerve testing)
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Acute haemodynamic deterioration: vasovagal, tamponade (pericardial effusion), VF, dissection, vessel perforation
⚠ Radiation exposure — wear lead apron + thyroid shield; step back when feasible
Vascular access complications: haematoma, retroperitoneal bleed, AV fistula, pseudoaneurysm
TAVI specific: rapid pacing → profound hypotension; paravalvular leak; conduction block (CHB risk)
MitraClip: TEE-guided — long procedure, risk of TEE injury
EP ablation: phrenic nerve injury (right-sided), oesophageal injury (LA posterior wall)
Pacemaker: pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, lead dislodgement
ICD: inappropriate shocks during testing — adequate sedation essential
equipmentChecklist: Defibrillator immediately available + pads applied for EP/VT
Emergency airway equipment (LMA, ETT) + difficult airway trolley
Lead aprons + thyroid shields for all team members

recovery.criteria: PCI/EP: arterial puncture site OK, distal pulses present, oriented
recovery.duration: PCI: 4-6 h bedrest. TAVI/MitraClip: ICU/HDU overnight
recovery.disposition: Diagnostic CAG: same-day. PCI: 1 night. TAVI/MitraClip: 1-3 nights ICU/HDU
recovery.warnings: Watch for: arterial site bleeding/haematoma, contrast nephropathy at 48-72h, distal limb ischaemia, conduction block (TAVI)

redFlags: Severe AS with critical low gradient (high TAVI mortality)
Severe COPD or PHTN (EP ablation under deep sedation risky)
Recent stroke (< 1 month) — TAVI bridging consideration
specialPopulations: Pregnancy — radiation shielding, lead apron over abdomen, time minimisation
Renal impairment — minimise contrast volume, iso-osmolar contrast
Severe LV dysfunction — etomidate induction, cautious volume, vasopressor ready
Pacemaker-dependent — magnet available, programming pre/post for diathermy
cardiac_cath.references: ESC TAVI Guidelines 2021; SCAI 2024 Cath Lab Sedation; HRS 2024 EP Procedure Guidelines; Faillace RT et al. JACC 2024

vascular_ir.label: Vascular IR / Interventional Radiology
techniques: Local + monitored sedation (most diagnostic + simple interventions)
General anaesthesia (EVAR, TEVAR, complex aortic, prolonged supine intolerable)

additional: Arterial line (EVAR, TEVAR, ruptured aneurysm, prolonged)
CSF drain (TEVAR for spinal cord protection)

drugCautions: Heparin systemic: 50-100 IU/kg loading — ACT target 200-300 sec for most cases
EVAR: heparin only after sheath placement (graft expansion)
TEVAR: spinal cord protection — MAP ≥ 90 mmHg, CSF drain target < 10 mmHg
Stroke thrombectomy: BP target SBP 140-180 (avoid hyper- and hypotension)
Embolisation: pain control (post-embolisation syndrome); fentanyl PCA post-procedure
Contrast same as Cath Lab — pre-medicate if allergy history
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Large-bore arterial access (24F EVAR, 22-24F TEVAR) — vascular complications high
⚠ TEVAR + arch: stroke risk — cerebral oximetry essential
⚠ TEVAR + thoracic: spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia) — CSF drain + MAP > 90
⚠ Ruptured AAA: aggressive resuscitation BUT permissive hypotension SBP 80-100 until clamp
Post-embolisation syndrome (fever, pain, nausea) — common after TACE/UAE
Stroke thrombectomy under conscious sedation often preferred (allows neuro assessment)
Long procedures: pressure injury risk, hypothermia, urinary retention

recovery.criteria: Haemodynamic stable, distal pulses, neuro intact (TEVAR/stroke), arterial puncture controlled
recovery.duration: EVAR: HDU 24h. TEVAR: ICU 24-72h. Simple IR: 4-6 h
recovery.disposition: Major aortic: ICU. Embolisation: ward. Diagnostic: same-day discharge
recovery.warnings: Watch for: graft endoleak, distal embolisation, contrast nephropathy, post-embolisation syndrome, paraplegia signs (TEVAR)

redFlags: Coagulopathy (active bleeding aside from AAA rupture)
Recent stroke + need for systemic anticoagulation
vascular_ir.references: SIR Sedation Guidelines 2018; ESVS 2024 Aortic Guidelines; SCAI 2024; AHA Stroke Thrombectomy 2024

gi_endoscopy.label: GI Endoscopy
gi_endoscopy.description: Diagnostic and therapeutic upper/lower GI endoscopy
techniques: Deep sedation / TIVA propofol (ERCP, ESD, EMR, complex therapeutic)
General anaesthesia + intubation (ERCP in high-risk aspiration, POEM, paediatric, prolonged ESD, prone position)

required: EtCO₂ (mandatory for moderate/deep sedation per ASA 2018)

inductionAgents.notes: Deep sedation; rapid recovery — preferred for ERCP/ESD
NEW (2020+) — rapid offset, flumazenil-reversible; emerging standard

drugCautions: Aspiration risk: NPO 6h solids, 2h clear fluids; suction immediately available
ERCP in prone position: airway access difficult — consider GA + ETT for high-risk
Variceal bleed: hypovolaemic — cautious propofol; ketamine adjunct; resuscitate first
Cirrhotic patients: reduced doses (altered drug clearance, increased sensitivity)
Elderly: titrate carefully; respiratory depression amplified
Sleep apnoea: consider CPAP recovery; deep sedation hazardous
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Hypoxia (most common adverse event in NORA per ASA Closed Claims)
⚠ Aspiration — particularly upper GI procedures, recent food, GI bleed, gastroparesis
⚠ Bowel perforation (rare but emergent — peritoneal signs, sudden pain, sepsis)
Splanchnic absorption: lidocaine throat spray + IV drugs — toxicity risk in young/elderly
ERCP-specific: pancreatitis post-procedure (3-15%); cholangitis if obstruction not relieved
POEM: pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum from CO₂ insufflation
Vagal stimulation during scope passage → bradycardia, hypotension
equipmentChecklist: Reversal agents: naloxone 0.4 mg, flumazenil 0.5 mg, sugammadex if rocuronium used
Recovery area with O₂ + pulse oximetry

recovery.criteria: Modified Aldrete ≥ 9; PADSS ≥ 9 for outpatient discharge
recovery.duration: 30-60 min for sedation; 1-2 h for deep sedation/GA
recovery.disposition: Outpatient: home with escort, no driving 24h. ERCP/ESD: often overnight observation
recovery.warnings: Watch for: delayed bleeding (24-48h), perforation signs (peritonism), post-ERCP pancreatitis (severe abdominal pain + amylase rise), aspiration pneumonitis

redFlags: Active GI bleed — high aspiration risk
Severe COPD with hypercapnia (deep sedation risky)
ASA IV-V — consider GA in OR setting
gi_endoscopy.references: ASA Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation 2018; BSGE/JAG Sedation Guidelines 2023; ESGE/ESGENA Curriculum 2024

tee_lab.label: TEE Lab
techniques: General anaesthesia + ETT (rare — hostile airway, agitated patient)

inductionAgents.notes: Brief deep sedation for TEE probe insertion + cardioversion shock

drugCautions: Anticoagulation: AF cardioversion requires LAA thrombus exclusion (TEE) OR ≥ 3 weeks therapeutic anticoag
Aspiration risk: NPO 6h solids, 2h clear fluids
Phenylephrine drawn for cardioversion-induced hypotension
Synchronised shock: 100-200 J biphasic for AF; 50-100 J for atrial flutter
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Oesophageal injury: perforation rare but devastating (< 0.1%)
⚠ Dysphagia/odynophagia post-procedure
Cardioversion: arrhythmia (VF/asystole) — ensure pads + crash cart
Failed cardioversion: amiodarone load + reattempt
Awake cardioversion painful — adequate sedation essential

recovery.criteria: Aldrete ≥ 9, no dysphagia/throat pain beyond expected
recovery.disposition: Outpatient discharge with escort; if cardioverted — anticoag plan documented
recovery.warnings: Watch for: oesophageal pain (perforation), dysphagia, post-cardioversion arrhythmia, embolic stroke

redFlags: Inadequate anticoagulation for cardioversion (AF > 48h without proper coverage)
tee_lab.references: EACVI/ASE TEE Guidelines 2022; ESC AF Guidelines 2024 (cardioversion); BSE Sedation for TEE Guidelines 2022

mri_suite.label: MRI Suite
mri_suite.description: Sedation/anaesthesia for MRI in adults and children
mri_suite.typicalSetting: Outpatient mostly; inpatient critically ill rare
techniques: Conscious sedation (oral chloral hydrate paeds — historic, less now)
General anaesthesia + LMA or ETT (uncooperative adults, prolonged scans, ICU patients)
Inhalational induction in paeds (sevoflurane via MR-compatible circuit)

inductionAgents.dose: Load 1-2 mcg/kg over 10 min, infusion 0.5-1 mcg/kg/h

inductionAgents.notes: Paeds inhalational induction with MR-compatible vaporiser
Paeds combative; avoid in raised ICP

drugCautions: ⚠ ALL equipment must be MR-compatible — verify before scan starts
Long extension tubing for IV (5-10 m) — calculate dead space
Long ETCO₂ sampling line — increased response delay
Hypothermia risk in paeds — pre-warm + active warming
Gadolinium contrast: avoid in eGFR < 30 (NSF risk)
If anaphylaxis: MOVE PATIENT OUT of MR room before resuscitation (defib MR-incompatible)
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Magnetic field hazards: ferromagnetic objects projectile risk; pacemaker/ICD interference
⚠ Distance from anaesthetist — limited access; use MR-compatible monitor + remote viewing
⚠ Contrast: gadolinium-related anaphylaxis rare but serious
Burns: ECG leads coiled or with skin contact — risk of RF heating
Hearing protection essential (noise > 100 dB)
Loss of motion = scan repeat — sedation depth critical (BIS useful)
Quench: rare emergency — evacuation, helium asphyxiation risk
equipmentChecklist: Long IV extension + EtCO₂ sampling line
Patient transfer trolley to OUT-OF-MAGNET resuscitation area
MR safety check completed (no implants, pacemaker compatibility)

recovery.duration: 30-60 min for sedation; 1-2 h for GA
recovery.warnings: Watch for: emergence delirium (paeds with sevo), gadolinium delayed reactions, hypothermia (paeds)

specialPopulations: Paediatric — most common NORA MRI; consider parent presence at induction
Critically ill — minimal monitoring possible, ICU transfer protocol
Pregnancy — gadolinium avoided in 1st trimester; sedation generally safe in 2nd/3rd
mri_suite.references: ACR-ASNR-SPR Guidelines for MRI Safety 2024; ASA NORA Statement 2024; AAGBI MRI Sedation 2019

ct_radiology.label: CT / Radiology
ct_radiology.description: Sedation for CT or general radiology procedures
drugCautions: Iodinated contrast: hold metformin 48h post if eGFR < 60
Contrast nephropathy: hydration 1 mL/kg/h pre/post in CKD
Severe contrast allergy: pre-medicate prednisolone 30 mg PO 13h, 7h, 1h pre + diphenhydramine
Breath-hold required for chest CT — adequate sedation depth
RFA: pain at probe site — opioid analgesia + local anaesthetic infiltration
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Pneumothorax post-lung biopsy (10-20%) — confirm chest X-ray
⚠ Bleeding post-liver/kidney biopsy
⚠ Contrast extravasation
Distance from anaesthetist during scan — long extensions
Radiation: lead apron + thyroid shield
RFA: thermal injury to adjacent structures

recovery.criteria: Aldrete ≥ 9; biopsy/RFA: pain controlled, no bleeding signs
recovery.disposition: Outpatient discharge with escort; biopsy may need overnight if high-risk
recovery.warnings: Watch for: pneumothorax (lung biopsy), bleeding (liver/kidney), contrast nephropathy at 48-72h

ct_radiology.references: ASA NORA Statement 2024; ACR Contrast Manual 2024; SIR Sedation 2018

bronchoscopy.label: Bronchoscopy Suite
techniques: Local + light sedation (flexible diagnostic — midazolam + lidocaine spray)
General anaesthesia + ETT/LMA (rigid bronch, stent, cryotherapy, massive haemoptysis)

additional: Arterial line (massive haemoptysis, severe respiratory failure)

drugCautions: ⚠ Lidocaine total dose — splanchnic absorption + topical add up; max 5 mg/kg (350 mg in 70 kg)
Aspiration risk: NPO 6h solids, 2h clear fluids
Asthma/COPD: bronchodilator pre-treatment; ketamine adjunct useful
Massive haemoptysis: lateral position (bleeding side down); rigid bronchoscopy + tamponade
EBUS: prolonged motionless period — propofol TIVA preferred over conscious sedation
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Hypoxia (most common adverse event) — use HFNO 30-50 L/min when possible
⚠ Bronchospasm — particularly in asthma, COPD
⚠ Pneumothorax post-TBB (3-5%) — confirm CXR
⚠ Bleeding post-biopsy (especially TBB, EBUS-TBNA)
Vagal stimulation → bradycardia, hypotension during scope passage
Foreign body removal: aspiration risk if dislodged distally
Rigid bronch: dental injury, vocal cord injury

recovery.criteria: Aldrete ≥ 9; gag reflex returned; no respiratory distress
recovery.disposition: Outpatient discharge with escort; TBB usually overnight if pneumothorax risk
recovery.warnings: Watch for: pneumothorax (TBB), delayed bleeding, post-procedure fever (BAL — common 24-48h), aspiration

redFlags: Severe hypoxia at baseline (SpO₂ < 90% on supplemental O₂)
bronchoscopy.references: BTS Bronchoscopy Guidelines 2013 (updates pending); ACCP/ATS EBUS Guidelines 2020; AAGBI 2019

icu_procedures.label: ICU Procedures
icu_procedures.description: Bedside procedures in critically ill patients
techniques: Deep sedation + neuromuscular block (tracheostomy, ECMO cannulation)

inductionAgents.notes: Haemodynamic instability, asthma; avoid in raised ICP
Tracheostomy, ECMO cannulation; reverse with sugammadex

drugCautions: Critically ill — reduced clearance, altered protein binding, drug accumulation
Renal/hepatic failure: drug dose adjustments mandatory
Inotropes/vasopressors often pre-existing — anticipate haemodynamic shifts
Pre-existing ETT — confirm adequate sedation/paralysis before tracheostomy
Anticoagulation: DOAC/heparin/LMWH timing — bridge if needed for line/drain
Cardioversion: synchronised 100-200 J biphasic; check K⁺, Mg²⁺, INR pre
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Haemodynamic instability common — vasopressors immediately ready
⚠ Tracheostomy: bleeding (anterior jugular, thyroid), tube misplacement, airway loss
⚠ Central line: pneumothorax (subclavian), arterial puncture, air embolism
⚠ ECMO cannulation: vessel injury, malposition, recirculation
Pericardiocentesis: cardiac/coronary perforation; arrhythmia
Multidisciplinary team essential (intensivist + proceduralist + anaesthetist)

recovery.criteria: Returned to baseline ICU sedation depth; haemodynamics stable
recovery.warnings: Watch for: bleeding (tracheostomy, lines), pneumothorax (subclavian, drain), tube displacement, infection

redFlags: Severe coagulopathy (INR > 2, platelets < 50) for invasive procedures
Severe hypotension on max vasopressors (ECMO consideration)
Difficult airway + need for general anaesthesia
icu_procedures.references: SCCM ICU Procedure Guidelines 2023; ANZICS Tracheostomy Guidelines 2020; ELSO ECMO Cannulation 2024

dental.label: Dental / Oral Surgery
dental.typicalSetting: Outpatient mostly; complex/paeds may be inpatient
techniques: Local anaesthesia + light oral/IV sedation (most adult)
Deep IV sedation (multiple extractions, anxious adult)
General anaesthesia + nasal intubation (paeds, complex, special needs)

inductionAgents.dose: Oral 0.5 mg/kg paeds (max 20 mg) / IV 0.02-0.05 mg/kg

drugCautions: Throat pack ESSENTIAL — count IN/OUT, document
Shared airway with surgeon — communication critical
Lidocaine for local: max 4.4 mg/kg with adrenaline (300 mg adult); 7 mg/kg with adrenaline absolute max
Articaine (popular dental LA): max 7 mg/kg with adrenaline
Adrenaline-containing LA: limit to 0.2 mg total in cardiac patients
Aspiration risk from blood/saliva in pharynx — head-down + suction
Paeds: weight-based dosing essential; consider rectal/oral pre-medication
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Shared airway — clear communication with dental team
⚠ Aspiration of blood, debris, broken instruments
⚠ Throat pack retention (sentinel event)
⚠ Nasotracheal tube for prolonged surgery — RAE preferred
Postoperative bleeding — pressure + adrenaline-soaked gauze
Trismus — limits airway access
PONV high incidence (swallowed blood) — ondansetron + dexamethasone
equipmentChecklist: Nasal RAE tube (if nasal intubation planned)

recovery.criteria: Aldrete ≥ 9; pain controlled; no active bleeding
recovery.disposition: Outpatient discharge with escort; soft diet; analgesia plan
recovery.warnings: Watch for: post-op bleeding, swelling/airway compromise, PONV, dental pain, dry socket (extraction)

redFlags: Difficult airway predictors (Mallampati IV, micrognathia, syndromes)
specialPopulations: Paediatric — most common population; consider parent presence
Special needs adult — pre-procedure assessment essential
Pregnancy — local + minimal sedation preferred 2nd trimester
dental.references: SAAD UK Dental Sedation 2020; AAPD Behavior Guidance 2023; AAOMS Anesthesia Practice 2024

pain_clinic.label: Pain Clinic

inductionAgents.notes: Anxiolysis; avoid for blocks needing patient response

drugCautions: ⚠ ASRA Anticoagulation Guidelines 2018 STRICT — neuraxial procedures
Aspirin: continue most procedures (low risk)
Clopidogrel: hold 7 days for high-risk neuraxial (epidural steroid lumbar OK)
Warfarin: hold 5 days, INR < 1.4
DOACs: hold 24-48h based on eGFR + procedure risk
LMWH: prophylactic — last dose 12h prior; therapeutic — 24h prior
Steroid (depo-medrol, triamcinolone): max 80 mg single injection
Avoid particulate steroids in cervical transforaminal (stroke risk)
Local anaesthetic doses — standard LA toxicity rules apply
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Intravascular injection (particulate steroid → stroke/spinal cord infarct in cervical transforaminal)
⚠ Dural puncture → headache, total spinal anaesthesia
⚠ Epidural haematoma if anticoagulation inadequately held
⚠ Infection — strict asepsis, masks, gowns
Vasovagal syncope common during procedure
Allergy: contrast (some procedures use), local anaesthetic
RFA: thermal injury to nerves; transient neuritis
SCS: lead migration, pain at IPG site

recovery.criteria: Aldrete ≥ 9; ambulatory; no neuro deficit; injection site OK
recovery.disposition: Outpatient discharge with escort; written instructions
recovery.warnings: Watch for: epidural haematoma signs (back pain + neuro deficit URGENT MRI), post-dural puncture headache, infection (3-7 days), worsening pain

redFlags: Severe stenosis at injection level (cord at risk)
pain_clinic.references: ASRA Anticoagulation Guidelines 2018; ASRA Pain Medicine Sedation 2023; SIS 2024 Practice Guidelines

neonatal_paeds.label: Neonatal / Paediatric Off-floor
neonatal_paeds.description: Procedures in neonates and children outside OR
techniques: Awake sedation neonate (often inadequate — consider GA)

inductionAgents.dose: Bolus 2-3 mg/kg (higher in paeds), infusion 100-200 mcg/kg/min
inductionAgents.notes: Paeds higher doses; risk of propofol infusion syndrome in prolonged use

drugCautions: Weight-based dosing CRITICAL — verify with second clinician
Sevoflurane: emergence delirium 30% — consider clonidine 1 mcg/kg or dexmedetomidine
Propofol infusion syndrome — avoid > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48h
Ketamine: avoid in raised ICP, age < 3 months
Caudal block: bupivacaine 0.25% 0.5 mL/kg (sacral) up to 1 mL/kg (mid-thoracic). ⚠ MAX 2 mg/kg total — verify volume × concentration ≤ 2 mg/kg before injection
Neonate: hypoglycaemia risk — IV dextrose 4-6 mg/kg/min
Hypothermia: pre-warm room, blankets, warm IV fluids, active warming
Air embolism: meticulous IV de-airing
procedureConcerns: ⚠ Hypothermia — neonates lose heat rapidly
⚠ Hypoglycaemia in neonates — check glucose hourly
⚠ Difficult IV access — consider IO if emergency
⚠ Difficult airway: large head, large tongue, cephalad larynx
Aspiration: gastric volume often higher proportionally
PONV: ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg + dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
Emergence delirium with sevo — clonidine prophylaxis useful
Pain assessment: FLACC scale (preverbal), Wong-Baker FACES
equipmentChecklist: Paeds-sized: ETT (cuffed and uncuffed sizes), LMA, masks, OPA/NPA
Paeds laryngoscope (Miller blade for neonate, Macintosh older)
Active warming (forced air, fluid warmer, overhead heater for neonate)
Parent present at induction option (if appropriate)

recovery.criteria: Modified Aldrete (paeds-adjusted); awake + age-appropriate response; pain controlled
recovery.duration: 30-60 min for procedural sedation; 1-2 h for GA
recovery.disposition: Discharge per protocol — escort, fluid intake, urination
recovery.warnings: Watch for: emergence delirium, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, post-op vomiting, pain

redFlags: Severe congenital heart disease without cardiac anaesthesia expertise
Recent URI in young child (< 4 weeks) — bronchospasm risk
Difficult airway syndromes (Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins)
Severe prematurity / former preterm with apnoea history (< 60 weeks PCA)
Active infection requiring transfer to OR
specialPopulations: Neonate (< 28 days) — specialist neonatal anaesthetist preferred
Ex-premature — apnoea monitoring 12-24h post-procedure if < 60 weeks PCA
Down syndrome — atlanto-axial instability, OSA, congenital heart
Cerebral palsy — GORD risk, respiratory compromise
neonatal_paeds.references: APAGBI Guidelines 2024; SAMBA Paediatric Sedation 2023; AAP Sedation 2019; APA UK 2024
